Show code
library(tidyverse)
library(lme4)
library(easystats)
source(here::here("R", "item-analysis.R"))

title: Item Functioning Across Instructors - Spring 2026
section: What is the variance in difficulty for each question for each instructior
text:
What is the variance in difficulty for each question for each instructior
The distance of each point from the line is difficulty_index - pooled_difficulty, so a histogram of this difference per instructor shows the variance directly.


Show code
by_instructor <- by_instructor |>
  mutate(diff_from_pooled = difficulty_index - pooled_difficulty)

spread_summary <- by_instructor |>
  summarise(
    n_items = n(),
    median_students = median(answered_student_count),
    mean_diff = mean(diff_from_pooled, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_diff = sd(diff_from_pooled, na.rm = TRUE),
    sampling_sd = sqrt(mean(variance / answered_student_count, na.rm = TRUE)),
    .by = instructor
  )

ggplot(by_instructor, aes(x = diff_from_pooled)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.05, fill = "#4C72B0", color = "white", alpha = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  facet_wrap(~instructor, ncol = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Instructor Difficulty Minus Pooled Difficulty",
    x = "Difference (positive = easier for this instructor's students)",
    y = "Items"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"), panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

title: Item Functioning Across Instructors - Spring 2026
section: Does item difficulty depend on instructor?
text:
Does item difficulty depend on instructor?
The variance is tested at its boundary (zero), so the reported p-value is conservative. Halving it gives the usual correction.


Show code
test_likelihoodratio(m0, m1)


# Likelihood-Ratio-Test (LRT) for Model Comparison (ML-estimator)

Name |    Model | df | df_diff | Criterion | Chi2 |     p
---------------------------------------------------------
m0   | glmerMod |  8 |         |  24941.99 |      |      
m1   | glmerMod |  9 |       1 |  24932.86 | 9.13 | 0.003


Adding a random intercept for item X instructor improved fit, \(\chi^2(1) = 9.13, p = .001\).


Show code
model_parameters(m1, effects = "random")


# Random Effects

Parameter                       | Coefficient | 95% CI
------------------------------------------------------
SD (Intercept: item:instructor) |        0.20 |       
SD (Intercept: id)              |        0.82 |       
SD (Intercept: item)            |        0.93 |       


Show code
icc(m1, by_group = TRUE)


# ICC by Group

Group           |   ICC
-----------------------
item:instructor | 0.008
id              | 0.137
item            | 0.178


Exam items differed in difficulty by a SD of 0.93 logits. For a typical Marshall student on a typical Exam 1 item, the odds of a correct answer are 3.77 (\(\ln(3.77) = 1.33\)), or a probability of .79. An item 1 SD easier than average has 2.53 times the odds of a correct answer (\(\exp(0.93) = 2.53\)), or \(P = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(1.33 + 0.93)}} = \frac{1}{1 + 0.104} = .906\) or 90.6%. An item 1 SD harder than average has 0.395 times the odds of a correct answer (\(\exp(-0.93) = \frac{1}{e^{0.93}} = \frac{1}{2.53} = 0.395\)), or \(P = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(1.33 - 0.93)}} = \frac{1}{1 + 0.670} = .599\) or 59.9%.
Students differed in ability by a SD of 0.82 logits. Using the same baseline, a student 1 SD above the mean has 2.27 times the odds of a correct answer (\(\exp(0.82) = 2.27\)), or \(P = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(1.33 + 0.82)}} = \frac{1}{1 + 0.116} = .896\) or 89.6%. A student 1 SD below the mean has 0.44 times the odds of a correct answer (\(\exp(-0.82) = \frac{1}{e^{0.82}} = \frac{1}{2.27} = 0.44\)), or \(P = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(1.33 - 0.82)}} = \frac{1}{1 + 0.601} = .625\) or 62.5%.
Item difficulty shifted for a given instructor’s students by a SD of 0.20 logits. Using the same baseline, an item 1 SD easier for one instructor’s students than its overall difficulty would predict has 1.22 times the odds of a correct answer (\(\exp(0.20) = 1.22\)), or \(P = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(1.33 + 0.20)}} = \frac{1}{1 + 0.217} = .822\) or 82.2%. An item 1 SD harder for one instructor’s students has 0.819 times the odds of a correct answer (\(\exp(-0.20) = \frac{1}{e^{0.20}} = \frac{1}{1.22} = 0.819\)), or \(P = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(1.33 - 0.20)}} = \frac{1}{1 + 0.323} = .756\) or 75.6%.
Exam item account for 17.8% of the variance in answering correctly, student differences account for 13.7%, and only 0.8% of the variance in answering correctly is due to instructor specific item shifts.

title: Item Functioning Across Instructors - Spring 2026
text:
Instructor differences in overall performance


Show code
model_parameters(m1, effects = "fixed", exponentiate = TRUE)


# Fixed Effects

Parameter            | Odds Ratio |   SE |       95% CI |     z |      p
------------------------------------------------------------------------
(Intercept)          |       3.77 | 0.58 | [2.79, 5.11] |  8.59 | < .001
exam [exam_02]       |       1.31 | 0.19 | [0.98, 1.75] |  1.82 | 0.068 
exam [exam_03]       |       0.66 | 0.10 | [0.49, 0.88] | -2.80 | 0.005 
instructor [okomeng] |       1.06 | 0.17 | [0.78, 1.44] |  0.39 | 0.699 
instructor [wood]    |       1.20 | 0.19 | [0.88, 1.63] |  1.15 | 0.250 
instructor [wu]      |       0.88 | 0.14 | [0.65, 1.19] | -0.86 | 0.389 


Each instructor is compared with Marshall on the same exam, and each exam with Exam 1 for the same instructor. A typical Marshall student on a typical Exam 1 item has odds of 3.77 to 1 of answering correctly (OR = 3.77, SE = 0.58, 95% CI [2.79, 5.11]), a probability of .79. Exam 2 items had 31% higher odds of a correct answer than Exam 1 items (OR = 1.31, SE = 0.19, 95% CI [0.98, 1.75], p = .068), a probability of .83 for a typical Marshall student, though the interval includes 1. Exam 3 items had 34% lower odds of a correct answer than Exam 1 items (OR = 0.66, SE = 0.10, 95% CI [0.49, 0.88], p = .005), a probability of .71.
Compared to Marshall’s students on the same exam, Okomeng’s students had 6% higher odds of answering correctly (OR = 1.06, SE = 0.17, 95% CI [0.78, 1.44], p = .699; probability .80 on Exam 1), Wood’s students had 20% higher odds (OR = 1.20, SE = 0.19, 95% CI [0.88, 1.63], p = .250; probability .82), and Wu’s students had 12% lower odds (OR = 0.88, SE = 0.14, 95% CI [0.65, 1.19], p = .389; probability .77). No instructor’s students differed significantly from Marshall’s. Only Exam 3 differed significantly from Exam 1.

title: Item Drift Between Semesters - Fall 2025 vs. Spring 2026
section: Does item difficulty drift between semesters?
text:
Does item difficulty drift between semesters?
The variance is tested at its boundary (zero), so halve the reported p-value.


Show code
test_likelihoodratio(d0, d1)


# Likelihood-Ratio-Test (LRT) for Model Comparison (ML-estimator)

Name |    Model | df | df_diff | Criterion |    Chi2 |      p
-------------------------------------------------------------
d0   | glmerMod | 12 |         |  41111.80 |         |       
d1   | glmerMod | 13 |       1 |  40035.30 | 1076.50 | < .001


Allowing item difficulty to differ by semester improved fit substantially, \(\chi^2(1) = 1076.5, p < .001\). Items shifted between semesters beyond the average exam by semester shift.


Show code
model_parameters(d1, effects = "random")


# Random Effects

Parameter                     | Coefficient | 95% CI
----------------------------------------------------
SD (Intercept: student)       |        0.70 |       
SD (Intercept: item:semester) |        0.72 |       
SD (Intercept: item)          |        0.86 |       


Show code
icc(d1, by_group = TRUE)


# ICC by Group

Group         |   ICC
---------------------
student       | 0.097
item:semester | 0.103
item          | 0.147


Exam items differed in difficulty by a SD of 0.86 logits. This is the part of item difficulty that holds across both semesters. For a typical Marshall student on a typical Exam 1 item in spring, the odds of a correct answer are 3.97 (\(18.06 \times 0.22 = 3.97\); \(\ln(3.97) = 1.38\)), or a probability of .80. An item 1 SD easier than average has 2.36 times the odds of a correct answer (\(\exp(0.86) = 2.36\)), or \(P = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(1.38 + 0.86)}} = \frac{1}{1 + 0.106} = .904\) or 90.4%. An item 1 SD harder than average has 0.42 times the odds of a correct answer (\(\exp(-0.86) = \frac{1}{e^{0.86}} = \frac{1}{2.36} = 0.42\)), or \(P = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(1.38 - 0.86)}} = \frac{1}{1 + 0.595} = .627\) or 62.7%.
Item difficulty shifted within a given semester by a SD of 0.72 logits, beyond that exam’s average fall-to-spring shift. Using the same baseline, an item 1 SD easier in one semester than its overall difficulty would predict has 2.05 times the odds of a correct answer (\(\exp(0.72) = 2.05\)), or \(P = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(1.38 + 0.72)}} = \frac{1}{1 + 0.122} = .891\) or 89.1%. An item 1 SD harder in one semester has 0.49 times the odds of a correct answer (\(\exp(-0.72) = \frac{1}{e^{0.72}} = \frac{1}{2.05} = 0.49\)), or \(P = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(1.38 - 0.72)}} = \frac{1}{1 + 0.517} = .659\) or 65.9%.
Students differed in ability by a SD of 0.70 logits. Using the same baseline, a student 1 SD above the mean has 2.01 times the odds of a correct answer (\(\exp(0.70) = 2.01\)), or \(P = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(1.38 + 0.70)}} = \frac{1}{1 + 0.125} = .889\) or 88.9%. A student 1 SD below the mean has 0.50 times the odds of a correct answer (\(\exp(-0.70) = \frac{1}{e^{0.70}} = \frac{1}{2.01} = 0.50\)), or \(P = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(1.38 - 0.70)}} = \frac{1}{1 + 0.507} = .664\) or 66.4%.

title: Item Drift Between Semesters - Fall 2025 vs. Spring 2026
text:
Overall semester differences
semester [spring] is the shift on Exam 1. The exam × semester terms show whether that shift differed on Exams 2 and 3.


Show code
model_parameters(d1, effects = "fixed", exponentiate = TRUE)


# Fixed Effects

Parameter                          | Odds Ratio |   SE |         95% CI
-----------------------------------------------------------------------
(Intercept)                        |      18.06 | 2.61 | [13.60, 23.98]
exam [exam_02]                     |       1.29 | 0.24 | [ 0.90,  1.84]
exam [exam_03]                     |       0.95 | 0.18 | [ 0.65,  1.38]
semester [spring]                  |       0.22 | 0.03 | [ 0.17,  0.29]
instructor [baber]                 |       1.01 | 0.12 | [ 0.81,  1.27]
instructor [okomeng]               |       1.03 | 0.10 | [ 0.85,  1.23]
instructor [wood]                  |       1.12 | 0.11 | [ 0.93,  1.35]
instructor [wu]                    |       0.84 | 0.10 | [ 0.67,  1.05]
exam [exam_02] × semester [spring] |       0.99 | 0.17 | [ 0.70,  1.39]
exam [exam_03] × semester [spring] |       0.71 | 0.13 | [ 0.50,  1.00]

Parameter                          |      z |      p
----------------------------------------------------
(Intercept)                        |  20.02 | < .001
exam [exam_02]                     |   1.39 | 0.165 
exam [exam_03]                     |  -0.27 | 0.786 
semester [spring]                  | -11.25 | < .001
instructor [baber]                 |   0.11 | 0.913 
instructor [okomeng]               |   0.26 | 0.794 
instructor [wood]                  |   1.20 | 0.230 
instructor [wu]                    |  -1.50 | 0.133 
exam [exam_02] × semester [spring] |  -0.08 | 0.939 
exam [exam_03] × semester [spring] |  -1.95 | 0.052 


Because the model includes an exam × semester interaction, the exam effects compare each exam with Exam 1 in fall only, and the semester effect compares spring with fall on Exam 1 only. Instructors are compared with Marshall, and the model assumes each instructor’s difference is the same across exams and semesters. A typical Marshall student on a typical fall Exam 1 item has odds of 18.06 to 1 of answering correctly (OR = 18.06, SE = 2.61, 95% CI [13.60, 23.98]), a probability of .95. In fall, Exam 2 items had 29% higher odds of a correct answer than Exam 1 items (OR = 1.29, SE = 0.24, 95% CI [0.90, 1.84], p = .165), a probability of .96 for a typical Marshall student, though the interval includes 1. In fall, Exam 3 items had 5% lower odds of a correct answer than Exam 1 items (OR = 0.95, SE = 0.18, 95% CI [0.65, 1.38], p = .786), a probability of .94.
On Exam 1, spring odds were 78% lower than fall odds (OR = 0.22, SE = 0.03, 95% CI [0.17, 0.29], p < .001), a probability of .80. The spring drop on Exam 2 was about the same as on Exam 1 (OR = 0.99, SE = 0.17, 95% CI [0.70, 1.39], p = [from output]). The spring drop on Exam 3 was 29% larger in odds than on Exam 1 (OR = 0.71, SE = 0.13, 95% CI [0.50, 1.00], p = .052), though the interval reaches 1.
Compared to Marshall’s students, Baber’s students had 1% higher odds of answering correctly (OR = 1.01, SE = 0.12, 95% CI [0.81, 1.27], p = .913; probability .95 on fall Exam 1), Okomeng’s students had 3% higher odds (OR = 1.03, SE = 0.10, 95% CI [0.85, 1.23], p = .794; probability .95 on fall Exam 1), Wood’s students had 12% higher odds (OR = 1.12, SE = 0.11, 95% CI [0.93, 1.35], p = .230; probability .95 on fall Exam 1), and Wu’s students had 16% lower odds (OR = 0.84, SE = 0.10, 95% CI [0.67, 1.05], p = .133; probability .77 on spring Exam 1). Baber taught only in fall and Wu only in spring.


Show code
emmeans(d1, ~ semester | exam, type = "response") |>
  pairs(reverse = TRUE, infer = TRUE)


exam = exam_01:
 contrast      odds.ratio     SE  df asymp.LCL asymp.UCL null z.ratio p.value
 spring / fall      0.224 0.0298 Inf     0.173     0.291    1 -11.249 <0.0001

exam = exam_02:
 contrast      odds.ratio     SE  df asymp.LCL asymp.UCL null z.ratio p.value
 spring / fall      0.221 0.0325 Inf     0.166     0.295    1 -10.266 <0.0001

exam = exam_03:
 contrast      odds.ratio     SE  df asymp.LCL asymp.UCL null z.ratio p.value
 spring / fall      0.158 0.0243 Inf     0.117     0.214    1 -12.009 <0.0001

Results are averaged over the levels of: instructor 
Confidence level used: 0.95 
Intervals are back-transformed from the log odds ratio scale 
Tests are performed on the log odds ratio scale 


Post hoc contrasts compared spring with fall within each exam, averaged over instructors. Spring odds were lower on every exam: 78% lower on Exam 1 (OR = 0.22, SE = 0.03, 95% CI [0.17, 0.29], p < .001), 78% lower on Exam 2 (OR = 0.22, SE = 0.03, 95% CI [0.17, 0.30], p < .001), and 84% lower on Exam 3 (OR = 0.16, SE = 0.02, 95% CI [0.12, 0.21], p < .001). For a typical Marshall student, the probability of a correct answer fell from .95 to .80 on Exam 1, from .96 to .84 on Exam 2, and from .94 to .73 on Exam 3.
No instructor’s students differed significantly from Marshall’s. In fall, no exam differed significantly from Exam 1. Spring odds were significantly lower than fall odds on all three exams.


Show code

  as_tibble() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = exam, y = Probability, color = semester)) +
  geom_pointrange(
    aes(ymin = CI_low, ymax = CI_high),
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.4)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#4C72B0", "#C44E52", "#55A868")) +
  labs(
    title = "Predicted Probability of a Correct Answer by Exam and Semester",
    subtitle = "Typical student and item, averaged over instructors; bars are 95% CIs",
    x = "Exam",
    y = "Probability correct",
    color = "Semester"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey40"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )
